overview.title: Contents (continued): chapters 2 and 3
overview.main_topic: Table of contents entries for chapter 2 (the mathematical building blocks of neural networks) and most of chapter 3 (TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX and Keras).
overview.central_idea: This contents page shows how the book first builds the mathematical foundations (tensors, tensor operations, gradient-based optimization, backpropagation) and then introduces the three low-level frameworks the book supports, each covered with the same parallel structure.
overview.importance: It lets you see the dependency chain of the early book: chapter 2's tensors and gradients are what chapter 3's frameworks implement, and you can jump directly to the topic you need.
learning_objectives: Locate the sections on tensors, tensor operations, gradient descent and backpropagation in chapter 2.
See that TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are each introduced with the same three-part structure (first steps, end-to-end linear classifier, what makes it unique).
Convert the printed page numbers shown here into PDF page numbers (+24).

paragraphs.excerpt: Scalars (rank-0 tensors) 22 ■ Vectors (rank-1 tensors) 22 Matrices (rank-2 tensors)
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 2.2 'Data representations for neural networks' is broken down into scalars (rank-0), vectors (rank-1), matrices (rank-2), rank-3 and higher tensors, key attributes, manipulating tensors in NumPy, the notion of data batches, and real-world examples of data tensors (printed pp.22-26).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The book introduces tensors bottom-up by rank, then names their key attributes and shows how batches and real datasets map onto tensor shapes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Every model in the book consumes and produces tensors; knowing rank and shape conventions is a prerequisite for reading any code listing.

terminology.meaning: the number of axes of a tensor (a matrix has rank 2)
a slice of the dataset along the first (samples) axis processed together

connections: p.50: batches and the four common data tensor shapes (printed 26)

paragraphs.excerpt: Element-wise operations 29 ■ Broadcasting 30 Tensor product 32 ■ Tensor reshaping
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 2.3 'The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations' covers element-wise operations, broadcasting, the tensor product, tensor reshaping, and geometric interpretations of tensor operations and of deep learning (printed pp.29-38).
paragraphs.what_it_means: After representing data as tensors, the book shows the handful of operations a layer actually performs and then gives them a geometric reading (transformations of points in space).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The geometric view (deep learning as uncrumpling data manifolds) is a recurring intuition in the book.

terminology.meaning: virtually repeating a smaller tensor so it matches a larger one in an element-wise operation
the dot product generalized to tensors, e.g. matrix multiplication

connections: p.62: geometric interpretation of deep learning (printed 38)

paragraphs.excerpt: What’s a derivative? 41 ■ Derivative of a tensor operation: The gradient
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 2.4 'The engine of neural networks: Gradient-based optimization' lists: what's a derivative, the gradient, stochastic gradient descent, and backpropagation (printed pp.41-46).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The book builds from a single-variable derivative to gradients of tensor operations, then to the SGD update rule and the chain rule applied to computation graphs.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the core of how networks learn; every later training loop relies on it.

terminology.meaning: the derivative of a function of a tensor with respect to that tensor
applying the chain rule to a computation graph to obtain gradients efficiently

paragraphs.excerpt: Reimplementing our first example from scratch 53 Running one training step 55
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 2.5 'Looking back at our first example' contains reimplementing the example from scratch, running one training step, the full training loop, and evaluating the model (printed pp.53-58).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The chapter closes by rebuilding the MNIST model without high-level Keras training utilities, so every concept from 2.2-2.4 appears in working code.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This from-scratch version demystifies what fit() does and prepares for the custom training loops of chapter 7.

paragraphs.excerpt: First steps with TensorFlow 64 ■ An end-to-end example: A linear classifier
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 3.3 'Introduction to TensorFlow' (printed p.63) contains first steps with TensorFlow (64), an end-to-end linear classifier in pure TensorFlow (69), and what makes the TensorFlow approach unique (74).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The TensorFlow section is the first instance of the template the chapter reuses for each framework.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Comparing the same linear classifier across three frameworks is a deliberate teaching device that highlights their differences.

terminology.meaning: a model that separates classes with a linear decision boundary, used here as a minimal end-to-end example

paragraphs.excerpt: First steps with PyTorch 75 ■ An end-to-end example: A linear classifier
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 3.4 'Introduction to PyTorch' (printed p.74) contains first steps with PyTorch (75), an end-to-end linear classifier in pure PyTorch (78), and what makes the PyTorch approach unique (81).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Same three-part structure as the TensorFlow section, applied to PyTorch.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Reading the sections side by side shows how the same math (chapter 2) is expressed in different APIs.

paragraphs.excerpt: First steps with JAX 82 ■ Tensors in JAX 83 ■ Random
paragraphs.what_it_says: Section 3.5 'Introduction to JAX' (printed p.82) contains first steps with JAX, tensors in JAX, random number generation in JAX, an end-to-end linear classifier in pure JAX (88), and what makes the JAX approach unique (90).
paragraphs.what_it_means: JAX gets two extra subsections, on tensors and on random number generation, signalling that these work differently there than in TensorFlow or PyTorch.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Inference: JAX's functional style (explicit random keys, immutable arrays) is the reason these extra topics are needed.

terminology.meaning: a numerical computing library with automatic differentiation and compilation, one of the three backends Keras 3 supports

deeper.title: Using printed vs. PDF page numbers
deeper.body: The numbers printed in this table of contents are the book's own (printed) page numbers. In this companion, PDF page numbers are used for links. For the main body of the book, **PDF page = printed page + 24** (for example, chapter 2 starts on printed page 16, which is PDF p.40; chapter 3 starts on printed page 60, PDF p.84). This offset was checked against the chapter-opener pages; it is a property of this PDF, not something the book states.

misconceptions.claim: The page numbers in the contents are the PDF page numbers.
misconceptions.correction: They are printed page numbers. In this PDF the main body is offset by 24 pages (printed 16 = PDF p.40).

earlier.note: First contents page: preface, front matter and chapter 1.

later.note: Contents continue with section 3.6 (Keras) and chapters 4-5.
Chapter 2 opener: The mathematical building blocks of neural networks.
Section 2.5: looking back at the first example.
Chapter 3 opener: TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX and Keras.

takeaways: Chapter 2 builds the math in order: tensors → tensor operations → gradients and backpropagation → a from-scratch reimplementation.
Chapter 3 introduces TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX with an identical three-part structure, ending each with what makes it unique.
Printed page numbers in the contents map to PDF pages by adding 24.

questions.question: According to the contents, in which section does the book introduce backpropagation?
questions.explanation: 'Chaining derivatives: The Backpropagation algorithm' is listed under 2.4 (printed 46, PDF p.70). 2.2 is about tensors, 2.3 about operations like broadcasting, and 3.3 is about TensorFlow.

questions.question: What three subsections appear for each of TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX in chapter 3?
questions.answer: First steps with the framework; an end-to-end example (a linear classifier in the pure framework); and what makes that framework's approach unique.
questions.explanation: Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 all list these three entries; JAX adds 'Tensors in JAX' and 'Random number generation in JAX'.

questions.question: Why might the book reimplement the first MNIST example from scratch (section 2.5) right after explaining tensors and gradients?
questions.answer: So the reader sees every concept from 2.2-2.4 (tensors, tensor operations, gradients, SGD) at work in code, demystifying what Keras's high-level training does.
questions.explanation: Inference from the section titles: 'Reimplementing our first example from scratch', 'Running one training step', 'The full training loop'.

questions.question: Chapter 2 starts on printed page 16. On which PDF page is it?
questions.explanation: The body of this PDF is offset by 24 pages: 16 + 24 = 40.

questions.question: Looking at the list for section 2.2, can you already define rank, shape and dtype of a tensor? If not, which page would you read first?
questions.answer: Read 'Key attributes' (printed 23, PDF p.47) after the rank-by-rank introduction starting at printed 22 (PDF p.46).
